batchName: Early Rome & the Kingdom: The Foundation of an Empire (753-509 BCE) - Easy Batch 1
chapterName: Early Rome & the Kingdom: The Foundation of an Empire (753-509 BCE)

questions.question: According to tradition, what was unusual about the background of King Servius Tullius?
options: He was raised by a she-wolf
He was a Greek refugee from Troy
He was the son of a slave
questions.explanation: Tradition held that Servius was the son of a slave. He rose to marry the daughter of the previous king, Tarquinius Priscus.
questions.sourceQuote: According to tradition, Rome's sixth king, Servius Tullius, was the son of a slave who married the daughter of the previous king, Tarquinius Priscus.

questions.question: What does archaeology suggest about Rome's kings?
options: The kings were really Greek governors from Cumae
All seven kings are confirmed by royal inscriptions
Rome never had kings; they were invented by Livy
Rome did have kings, though the stories about them are doubtful
questions.explanation: Archaeology confirms that Rome had kings, but most scholars doubt the traditional stories about them. Modern historians are cautious because so few written sources survive.
questions.sourceQuote: Archaeology shows that Rome did have kings, but most scholars doubt the traditional stories about them.

questions.question: Which Latin town, said to be Romulus's birthplace, was destroyed by King Tullus Hostilius?
questions.explanation: The warlike Tullus Hostilius destroyed Alba Longa and moved its people to Rome. He also built a senate house that lasted for centuries.
questions.sourceQuote: He fought Rome's neighbours and destroyed Alba Longa, the Latin town said to be Romulus's birthplace, moving its people to Rome.

questions.question: According to legend, which hero held a bridge alone against the army of Lars Porsenna?
questions.explanation: Horatius held the bridge alone until it could be torn down. Porsenna, an Etruscan king from Clusium, had marched on Rome to help Tarquin return.
questions.sourceQuote: An Etruscan king, Lars Porsenna of Clusium, marched on Rome, but legend says the hero Horatius held a bridge alone until it could be torn down.

questions.question: What were the fasces, carried ahead of Rome's kings by their attendants?
options: A bundle of rods around an axe
A gilded eagle on a tall pole
A set of sacred temple keys
questions.explanation: The fasces were a bundle of rods around an axe that symbolised the king's power to punish. Twelve attendants carried them ahead of him.
questions.sourceQuote: Twelve attendants walked ahead of him carrying the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe that symbolised his power to punish.

questions.question: By about which date was Rome a true city, with a central forum, monumental buildings and public temples?
questions.explanation: By 600 BC the villages had fully merged into one city. Rome now had a central forum, monumental buildings and public temples.
questions.sourceQuote: By 600 BC the process was complete.

questions.question: Servius Tullius is credited with holding Rome's first what?
questions.explanation: Servius held Rome's first census and sorted citizens into five classes by wealth. His lasting fame rests on this reorganisation of Roman society.
questions.sourceQuote: He held Rome's first census, a count of citizens, and sorted people into five classes by wealth.

questions.question: Which year did the Romans officially give for the founding of their city?
questions.explanation: The scholar Varro worked out the official founding date of 753 BC. Romans celebrated it every year on 21 April.
questions.sourceQuote: The official founding date, worked out by the scholar Varro, was 753 BC, celebrated on 21 April.

questions.question: Romulus chose 100 leading men as advisers, called the "fathers". What did their descendants become?
questions.explanation: The descendants of Romulus's 100 "fathers" became the patricians, Rome's hereditary aristocracy. Romulus was also escorted by twelve attendants called lictors.
questions.sourceQuote: They were called the "fathers", and their descendants became the patricians, Rome's hereditary aristocracy.

questions.question: By around 1000 BC, what was the valley that later became the Roman Forum used for?
questions.explanation: Long before it became Rome's great public square, the Forum valley was a cemetery. Huts already stood on the nearby Palatine Hill by the 9th or 8th century BC.
questions.sourceQuote: By 1000 BC the valley that later became the Roman Forum, the city's great public square, was a cemetery.
